title: Limiter backpressure token-lease telemetry and chaos recovery playbook
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Problem:
Redwood has experienced several transient limiter outages and uneven burst absorption across regions during last quarter's high-traffic events. These incidents showed three classes of failure: silent token loss during lease handoff, poor observability into per-tenant live-credit state, and brittle recovery when a regional limiter pod restarts.

Goal:
Deliver a conservative, production-ready implementation that: (1) introduces a short-lived token-lease layer to make ownership explicit across replicas, (2) emits fine-grained telemetry required to correlate SLO violations to limiter state, and (3) codifies a chaos-tested recovery playbook that the ops team can run during incidents without risking cascading denial-of-service for high-tier customers.

Acceptance criteria:
- New token-lease protocol implemented for limiter proxies with backwards-compatible fallthrough to current credit model.
- Telemetry coverage: lease acquire/release events, lease renewal latency histogram, per-tenant admitted vs rejected tokens, and lease conflict counters.
- Automated chaos tests (regional restart, partition, and delayed lease renewals) pass in staging with no more than 5% client error spike for P1 customers.
- Runbook and one-click mitigation (scale-to-zero fallback and emergency soft-credits) documented and validated in runbook-drill.

Design summary:
We will layer a short TTL "lease token" on top of existing token credits. Each limiter replica will attempt to acquire a lease for tenant-shards it serves; leases are stored in a small, strongly-consistent metadata store (primary design uses our existing regional Redis cluster with a single-writer lease token pattern). Lease state is best-effort and ephemeral: when a lease cannot be acquired quickly, the proxy falls back to admitting a conservative per-tenant admission rate (configured per-SLO tier).

Key trade-offs considered:
- Strong consistency vs latency: we keep leases short (100-600ms) to avoid long acquisition stalls and accept occasional short-lived conflicts which metrics will surface.
- Centralized metadata store vs fully decentralized: centralizing to regional Redis simplifies correctness on failover but requires careful circuit-breaker rules to avoid overloading Redis under global floods.
- Conservative fallback vs risk of customer impact: fallbacks prioritize SLO-backed customers by applying weighted admission; lower-tier customers may see degraded traffic during metadata-store outages.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature-flagged deploy to staging (limiters in two non-prod regions).
2) Telemetry validation: ensure dashboards and tracing are capturing lease and conflict events.
3) Canary: enable for 5% of traffic in us-west only with canary SLA on runtime-1.20.
4) Progressive ramp across regions with automated rollback triggers tied to spike thresholds and error budgets.

Testing and validation:
- Unit + integration tests for lease races and renewals.
- Chaos matrix: (a) limiter pod restart, (b) Redis failover, (c) network partition between proxy and metadata store, (d) delayed lease grant.
- SLO regression tests against synthetic client traffic and heritage traffic replays.

Runbook highlights (short):
- Detection: dashboard triggers if lease_conflicts_per_minute > 50 and admitted_rate_drop > 20% for 10m.
- Immediate mitigation: flip feature-flag to conservative fallback OR enact emergency soft-credits for affected tenants.
- Recovery: sequentially restart limiter replicas with coordination window; avoid simultaneous restarts in multiple AZs.
- Post-incident: collect lease timelines and correlation IDs for root-cause analysis.
